modern:
Look, the month of flowers has come! March winds and April showers have done their work, and the earth is all decked out in beauty. Come, my soul, put on your holiday clothes and go out to gather garlands of heavenly thoughts. You know where to go, for “the beds of spices” are well known to you, and you have so often smelled the perfume of “the sweet flowers” that you’ll go straight to your well-beloved and find all loveliness, all joy in him. That cheek, once so roughly struck with a rod, often wet with tears of sympathy and then defiled with spit, that cheek, as it smiles with mercy, is like fragrant spice to my heart. You didn’t hide your face from shame and spitting, O Lord Jesus, and so I’ll find my dearest delight in praising you. Those cheeks were furrowed by the plow of grief, and streaked crimson with blood from your thorn-crowned forehead. Such marks of boundless love can’t help but charm my soul far more than “pillars of perfume.”

If I can’t see his whole face, I would look at his cheeks, for the smallest glimpse of him is wonderfully refreshing to my spiritual senses and gives a variety of delights. In Jesus I find not only fragrance, but a bed of spices; not one flower, but all kinds of sweet flowers. He is my rose and my lily, my heartsease and my cluster of henna. When he is with me, it’s May all year round, and my soul goes out to wash her happy face in the morning dew of his grace, and to delight herself with the singing of the birds of his promises. Precious Lord Jesus, let me truly know the blessedness that lives in lasting, unbroken fellowship with you. I’m a poor, worthless one whose cheek you have stooped to kiss! Oh, let me kiss you in return with the kisses of my lips.

modern:
Whatever beauty there may be in the material world, Jesus Christ has all of it in the spiritual world ten times over. Among flowers the rose is thought the sweetest, but Jesus is infinitely more beautiful in the garden of the soul than the rose can be in the gardens of earth. He takes first place as the fairest among ten thousand. He is the sun, and all others are the stars; the heavens and the day are dark compared with him, *for the King in his beauty surpasses all*. “I am the rose of *Sharon*.” This was the best and rarest of roses. Jesus isn’t just “the rose”; he is “the rose of Sharon,” just as he calls his righteousness “gold,” and then adds “the gold of Ophir”: the best of the best. He is truly lovely, and lovelier than anything else.

*There is variety in his charms.* The rose delights the eye, and its scent is pleasant and refreshing; in the same way, each of the soul’s senses, whether taste or touch, hearing, sight or spiritual smell, finds its proper satisfaction in Jesus. *Even the memory of his love is sweet.* Take the rose of Sharon, pull it apart petal by petal, and store the petals in the jar of memory, and you’ll find each petal fragrant long afterward, filling the house with perfume. Christ *satisfies the highest taste* of the most cultivated spirit to the full. The greatest lover of perfumes is quite satisfied with the rose; and when the soul has reached her highest level of true taste, she will still be content with Christ; no, she’ll be all the better able to appreciate him. Heaven itself has nothing that surpasses the rose of Sharon. What emblem can fully show his beauty? Human speech and earthly things fail to describe him. Earth’s choicest charms mixed together only faintly picture his overflowing preciousness. Blessed rose, bloom in my heart forever!

modern:
It’s a sweet and blessed event that will come to every believer in God’s own time: going home to be with Jesus. In a few more years the Lord’s soldiers, now fighting “the good fight of faith,” will be done with battle and will have entered into the joy of their Lord. But although Christ prays that his people may eventually be with him where he is, he doesn’t ask that they be taken straight from this world to heaven. He wants them to stay here. Yet how often the weary pilgrim prays, “O that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away and be at rest.” But Christ doesn’t pray like that. He leaves us in his Father’s hands, until, like fully ripe sheaves of grain, we are each gathered into our Master’s barn. Jesus doesn’t plead for us to be removed at once by death, for staying in the body is needed for others, even if it isn’t profitable for ourselves. He asks that we may be kept from evil, but he never asks for us to be admitted to the inheritance in glory until we’re of full age.

Christians often want to die when they have any trouble. Ask them why, and they’ll tell you, “Because we would be with the Lord.” We’re afraid it isn’t so much because they long to be with the Lord as because they want to be rid of their troubles; otherwise they’d feel the same wish to die at other times, when they aren’t under the pressure of trial. They want to go home not so much for the Savior’s company as to be at rest. Now, it’s quite right to desire to depart if we can do it in the same spirit Paul did, because being with Christ is far better; but the wish to escape trouble is a selfish one. Instead, let your care and wish be to glorify God by your life here as long as he pleases, even in the middle of toil and battle and suffering, and leave it to him to say when “it is enough.”

modern: Look at the epitaph of all those blessed saints who fell asleep before our Lord came! It doesn’t matter how else they died, whether of old age or by violence; this one point, which they all share, is the most worth recording: “they all died in faith.” They lived by faith; it was their comfort, their guide, their motive and their support. And in the same spiritual grace they died, ending their life’s song on the sweet note they had kept up so long. They didn’t die resting in the flesh or in their own achievements. They never moved on from the way they were first accepted by God, but held to the way of faith to the end. Faith is as precious to die by as to live by.

Dying in faith looks back to *the past*. They believed the promises that had gone before, and were sure their sins were blotted out through the mercy of God. Dying in faith has to do with *the present*. These saints were confident of their acceptance with God; they enjoyed the beams of his love and rested in his faithfulness. Dying in faith looks into *the future*. They fell asleep declaring that the Messiah would surely come, and that when he appeared on the earth in the last days, they would rise from their graves to see him. To them the pains of death were only the birth pangs of a better state. Take courage, my soul, as you read this epitaph. By grace your course is one of faith, and sight seldom cheers you; this has also been the path of the brightest and best. Faith was the orbit in which these stars of the first magnitude moved all the time they shone here, and you’re happy that it’s yours. Look again tonight to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith, and thank him for giving you the same precious faith as the souls now in glory.

modern:
Are you asking the reason for this, believer? Look up at your heavenly Father, and see how pure and holy he is. Do you know that one day you’re to be like him? Will you be shaped into his image easily? Won’t you need a great deal of refining in the furnace of affliction to purify you? Will it be easy to get rid of your sinful desires and make you perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect? Next, Christian, turn your eye *downward*. Do you know what enemies you have beneath your feet? You were once a servant of Satan, and no king willingly loses his subjects. Do you think Satan will leave you alone? No, he’ll always be at you, for he “goeth about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” So expect trouble, Christian, when you look beneath you.

Then look *around you*. Where are you? You’re in enemy country, a stranger and a temporary resident. The world isn’t your friend. If it is, then you’re not God’s friend, for whoever is the friend of the world is the enemy of God. You can be sure you’ll find enemies everywhere. When you sleep, think that you’re resting on the battlefield. When you walk, suspect an ambush in every hedge. As mosquitoes are said to bite strangers more than natives, so the trials of earth will be sharpest for you. Last of all, look *within you*, into your own heart, and see what’s there. *Sin* and *self* are still inside. Ah, if you had no devil to tempt you, no enemies to fight you and no world to trap you, you’d still find enough evil in yourself to be a painful trouble to you, for “the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.” So expect trouble, but don’t lose heart because of it, for God is with you to help and strengthen you. He has said, “I will be with thee in trouble; I will deliver thee and honour thee.”

modern:
Covenant blessings aren’t meant only to be looked at, but to be taken and used. Even our Lord Jesus is given to us for our present use. Believer, you don’t make use of Christ as you ought to. When you’re in trouble, why don’t you tell him all your grief? Doesn’t he have a sympathizing heart, and can’t he comfort and relieve you? No, you go around to all your friends except your best Friend, telling your story everywhere except into the bosom of your Lord. Are you weighed down with today’s sins? Here is a fountain filled with blood: use it, saint, use it. Has a sense of guilt come back on you? The pardoning grace of Jesus can be proved again and again. Come to him at once for cleansing. Are you grieving over your weakness? He is your strength; why not lean on him? Do you feel naked? Come here, soul: put on the robe of Jesus’ righteousness. Don’t stand looking at it; wear it. Strip off your own righteousness, and your own fears too, and put on the fine white linen, for it was meant to be *worn*.

Do you feel sick? Ring the night bell of prayer and wake up the Beloved Physician! He’ll give you the medicine that will revive you. You’re poor, but you have “a kinsman, a mighty man of wealth.” What! Won’t you go to him and ask him to give you some of his abundance, when he has given you this promise, that you’ll be a joint heir with him, and has handed over all that he is and all that he has to be yours? There’s nothing Christ dislikes more than for his people to make a showpiece of him and not use him. He loves to be put to work by us. The more burdens we put on his shoulders, the more precious he’ll be to us.

modern: One great besetting sin of ancient Israel was idolatry, and the spiritual Israel is troubled with a tendency to the same folly. Remphan’s star no longer shines, and the women no longer weep for Tammuz, but Mammon still pushes in his golden calf, and the shrines of pride aren’t abandoned. Self in various forms struggles to bring the chosen under its rule, and the flesh sets up its altars wherever it can find room for them. Favorite children are often the cause of much sin in believers. The Lord is grieved when he sees us doting on them beyond measure. They’ll live to be as great a curse to us as Absalom was to David, or they’ll be taken from us and leave our homes empty. If Christians want to grow thorns to stuff their sleepless pillows, let them dote on their dear ones.

It’s rightly said that “they are no gods,” for the objects of our foolish love are very doubtful blessings. The comfort they give us now is dangerous, and the help they can give in the hour of trouble is very small. So why are we so bewitched with empty things? We pity the poor heathen who worship a god of stone, and yet we worship a god of gold. Where is the great superiority of a god of flesh over one of wood? The principle, the sin, the folly is the same in either case, except that in ours the crime is worse, because we have more light and sin in the face of it. The heathen bows to a false god, but he has never known the true God. We commit two evils, since we forsake the living God and turn to idols. May the Lord cleanse us all from this grievous sin!

modern:
Peter earnestly urged the scattered saints to love each other “with a pure heart fervently,” and he wisely drew his argument not from the law, or nature, or philosophy, but from the high and divine nature God has planted in his people. A wise tutor of princes might work to create and nurture a kingly spirit and dignified behavior in them, finding his arguments in their position and family. In the same way, Peter looks on God’s people as heirs of glory, princes of the royal blood, descendants of the King of kings, earth’s truest and oldest aristocracy, and says to them, “See that ye love one another, because of your noble birth, being born of incorruptible seed; because of your pedigree, being descended from God, the Creator of all things; and because of your immortal destiny, for you shall never pass away, though the glory of the flesh shall fade, and even its existence shall cease.”

It would be good if, in a spirit of humility, we recognized the true dignity of our reborn nature and lived up to it. What is a Christian? Compare him with a king, and he adds priestly holiness to royal dignity. A king’s royalty often lies only in his crown, but with a Christian it is poured into his inmost nature. Through his new birth he is as far above his fellows as a man is above the beast that perishes. Surely he ought to conduct himself in all his dealings as one who isn’t one of the crowd, but chosen out of the world, set apart by sovereign grace, written among “the peculiar people.” So he can’t grovel in the dust like others, or live the way the world’s citizens live. Believers in Christ, let the dignity of your nature and the brightness of your prospects compel you to hold fast to holiness and avoid even the appearance of evil.

modern:
What a sweet title: “My people!” What a cheering revelation: “Their God!” How much meaning is packed into those two words, “My people”! Here is *specialness*. The whole world is God’s; the heaven, even the heaven of heavens, is the Lord’s, and he reigns among the children of men. But of those he has chosen, whom he has bought for himself, he says what he doesn’t say of others: “My people.” In this word there is the idea of *ownership*. In a special way “the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.” All the nations on earth are his; the whole world is in his power; yet his people, his chosen, are more especially his possession, because he has done more for them than for others. He has bought them with his blood. He has brought them near to himself. He has set his great heart on them. He has loved them with an everlasting love, a love that many waters can’t quench, and that the turning of time will never be able to lessen in the least.

Dear friends, can you by faith see yourselves among that number? Can you look up to heaven and say, “My Lord and my God: mine by that sweet *relationship* which entitles me to call thee Father; mine by that hallowed *fellowship* which I delight to hold with thee when thou art pleased to manifest thyself unto me as thou dost not unto the world”? Can you read the inspired Book and find the title deeds of your salvation there? Can you read your title written in precious blood? Can you, by humble faith, take hold of Jesus’ garment and say, “My Christ”? If you can, then God says of you, and of others like you, “My people.” For if God is your God, and Christ your Christ, the Lord has a special, particular favor toward you; you are the object of his choice, accepted in his beloved Son.

modern:
Wisdom is a person’s true strength; under its guidance he best fulfills the purposes of his life. Handling the business of life wisely gives a person the richest enjoyment and the noblest work for his powers, and so through it he finds good in the fullest sense. Without wisdom, a person is like a wild donkey’s colt, running here and there, wasting strength that could be put to good use. Wisdom is the compass by which a person must steer across the trackless waste of life; without it he’s an abandoned ship, the plaything of winds and waves. A person must be wise and careful in a world like this, or he’ll find no good, but be led into countless troubles. The pilgrim will badly wound his feet among the briers in the wood of life if he doesn’t pick his steps with the greatest caution. Anyone in a wilderness full of gangs of robbers must handle things wisely if he wants to travel safely. If, trained by the Great Teacher, we follow where he leads, we’ll find good even in this dark place. There are heavenly fruits to be gathered this side of Eden’s arbors, and songs of paradise to be sung among the groves of earth.

But where will this wisdom be found? Many have dreamed of it but haven’t had it. Where will we learn it? Let’s listen to the voice of the Lord, for he has told the secret. He has shown the sons of men where true wisdom lies, and we have it in the text: “Whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he.” *The true way to handle a matter wisely is to trust in the Lord.* This is the sure thread through the most tangled mazes of life; follow it, and find eternal bliss. Whoever trusts in the Lord has a diploma in wisdom granted by inspiration: he is happy now, and he’ll be happier still above. Lord, in this sweet evening, walk with me in the garden and teach me the wisdom of faith.

modern:
Do you want a house for your soul? Do you ask, “What’s the price?” It’s something less than proud human nature will like to give. It’s without money and without price. Ah, you’d like to pay a respectable rent! You’d love to do something to earn Christ? Then you can’t have the house, for it is “without price.” Will you take my Master’s house on a lease for all eternity, with nothing to pay for it, nothing but the ground rent of loving and serving him forever? Will you take Jesus and “dwell in him”? Look, this house is furnished with everything you need. It’s filled with more riches than you’ll spend as long as you live. Here you can have close fellowship with Christ and feast on his love. Here are tables well stocked with food for you to live on forever. In it, when you’re tired, you can find rest with Jesus, and from it you can look out and see heaven itself.

Will you have the house? Ah, if you’re homeless, you’ll say, “I should like to have the house; but may I have it?” Yes; there’s the key, and the key is “Come to Jesus.” “But,” you say, “I am too shabby for such a house.” Never mind; there are clothes inside. If you feel guilty and condemned, come; and though the house is too good for you, Christ will make you good enough for the house before long. He’ll wash you and clean you, and you’ll yet be able to sing, “We dwell in him.” Believer, how very happy you are to have such a home! You’re greatly privileged, for you have a “strong habitation” where you’re always safe. And “dwelling in him,” you have not only a perfect and secure house, but an *everlasting* one. When this world has melted like a dream, our house will live on and stand, more lasting than marble, more solid than granite, self-existent as God, for it is God himself: “We dwell in him.”

modern:
*A short stay on earth will make heaven more heavenly.* Nothing makes rest so sweet as toil; nothing makes safety so pleasant as being exposed to alarm. The bitter quassia cups of earth will add relish to the new wine that sparkles in the golden bowls of glory. Our battered armor and scarred faces will make our victory above more glorious, when we’re welcomed to the seats of those who have overcome the world. We wouldn’t have full *fellowship with Christ* if we didn’t live here below for a while, for he was baptized with a baptism of suffering among men, and we must be baptized with the same if we want to share his kingdom. Fellowship with Christ is so honorable that the sharpest sorrow is a small price to pay for it. Another reason we linger here is *for the good of others*. We wouldn’t want to enter heaven until our work is done, and it may be that we’re still appointed to bring light to souls lost in darkness in the wilderness of sin.

No doubt our long stay here is also *for God’s glory*. A tested saint, like a well-cut diamond, sparkles brightly in the King’s crown. Nothing brings so much honor to a workman as a long, hard test of his work, which it comes through in triumph without giving way anywhere. We are God’s workmanship, and he will be glorified in us by our afflictions. It’s for the honor of Jesus that we endure the testing of our faith with holy joy. Let each of us give up our own longings to the glory of Jesus, and feel, “If my lying in the dust would elevate my Lord by so much as an inch, let me still lie among the pots of earth. If to live on earth for ever would make my Lord more glorious, it should be my heaven to be shut out of heaven.” Our time is fixed and settled by eternal decree. Let’s not be anxious about it, but wait patiently until the gates of pearl open.

modern: What a mass of hideous sickness must have been pushed in front of Jesus’ eyes! Yet we don’t read that he was disgusted; he patiently attended to every case. What a strange variety of ills must have gathered at his feet! What sickening ulcers and rotting sores! Yet he was ready for every new shape of that monster, evil, and conquered it in every form. Let the arrow fly from wherever it might, he put out its fiery power. The heat of fever or the cold of dropsy, the stupor of palsy or the rage of madness, the filth of leprosy or the darkness of eye disease: all felt the power of his word and fled at his command. In every corner of the field he triumphed over evil and received the homage of freed captives. He came, he saw, he conquered everywhere. It’s the same this morning. Whatever my own case may be, the beloved Physician can heal me; and whatever the state of others I may remember in prayer right now, I can hope in Jesus that he’ll be able to heal them of their sins. My child, my friend, my dearest one: I can have hope for each, for all, when I remember my Lord’s healing power. And for my own part, however hard my struggle with sins and weaknesses, I can still be of good cheer. He who walked the hospitals on earth still gives out his grace and works wonders among the sons of men. Let me go to him at once, in real earnest.

Let me praise him this morning as I remember how he worked his spiritual cures, which bring him the most fame. It was by taking our sicknesses on himself. “By his stripes we are healed.” The church on earth is full of souls healed by our beloved Physician, and the people of heaven itself confess that “He healed them all.” Come, then, my soul, spread abroad the power of his grace, and let it be “to the Lord for a name, for an everlasting sign which shall not be cut off.”

modern: Like many others, the disabled man had been waiting for a wonder to happen and a sign to be given. Wearily he watched the pool, but no angel came, or none came for him. Yet thinking it was his only chance, he kept waiting, and didn’t know that there was One near him whose word could heal him in a moment. Many are in the same plight. They’re waiting for some unusual emotion, some remarkable impression or heavenly vision; they wait in vain and watch for nothing. Even supposing remarkable signs are seen in a few cases, they’re rare, and no one has a right to look for them in his own case; especially no one who feels he’s too weak to make use of the moving of the water even if it came. It’s a very sad thought that tens of thousands are waiting right now in the use of means and ordinances and vows and resolutions, and have waited like this for ages, in vain, completely in vain. Meanwhile these poor souls forget the Savior who is here now, who tells them to look to him and be saved. He could heal them at once, but they’d rather wait for an angel and a wonder. Trusting him is the sure way to every blessing, and he deserves the most complete confidence; but unbelief makes them prefer the cold porches of Bethesda to the warm bosom of his love. Oh, that the Lord may turn his eye on the crowds who are in this state tonight! May he forgive the slights they put on his divine power, and call them by that sweet, compelling voice to rise from the bed of despair and, in the energy of faith, take up their bed and walk. O Lord, hear our prayer for all such people at this calm hour of sunset, and before the day breaks may they look and live.
Kind reader, is there anything in this reading for you?

modern:
Years are short to the happy and healthy; but thirty-eight years of disease must have dragged on very wearily through the life of the poor disabled man. So when Jesus healed him with a word, as he lay by the pool of Bethesda, he was delightfully *aware of a change*. In the same way the sinner who has been paralyzed with despair for weeks and months, and has wearily sighed for salvation, is very conscious of the change when the Lord Jesus speaks the word of power and gives joy and peace in believing. The evil taken away is too great to go without our noticing; the life given is too remarkable to be had and lie idle; and the change worked is too wonderful not to be seen.

Yet the poor man was *ignorant of who had cured him*. He didn’t know how sacred his person was, the offices he held, or the errand that had brought him among men. A heart can still know very little about Jesus and yet feel the power of his blood. We mustn’t be quick to condemn people for lack of knowledge; where we can see the faith that saves the soul, we must believe that salvation has been given. The Holy Spirit makes people repentant long before he makes them theologians; and whoever believes what he knows will soon know more clearly what he believes.

Ignorance is still an evil, though; for this poor man was badly *harassed by the Pharisees*, and wasn’t able to answer them at all. It’s good to be able to answer people who argue against the truth; but we can’t do that if we don’t know the Lord Jesus clearly and with understanding. The cure of his ignorance soon followed the cure of his illness, for he was *visited by the Lord in the temple*; and after that gracious showing of himself, he was *found testifying* that “it was Jesus who had made him whole.” Lord, if you have saved me, show me yourself, so that I may make you known to the people around me.

modern:
If we want to “acquaint ourselves with God, and be at peace” in the right way, we must know him as he has revealed himself: not only in *the oneness of his being*, but also in *the three persons of the Godhead*. God said, “Let us make man in our own image”; so let no one be content until he knows something of the “us” his being came from.

Try to know the Father. Bury your head against his heart in deep repentance, and confess that you’re not worthy to be called his son. Receive the kiss of his love; let the ring that is the token of his eternal faithfulness be on your finger; sit at his table and let your heart celebrate in his grace.

Then press on and try to know much about *the Son* of God, who is the brightness of his Father’s glory, and yet, stooping in grace beyond words, became man for our sakes. Know him in the unique mystery of his nature: eternal God, and yet a suffering, finite man. Follow him as he walks on the water with the tread of God, and as he sits by the well, tired as any man. Don’t be satisfied until you know much of Jesus Christ as your Friend, your Brother, your Husband, your all.

Don’t forget *the Holy Spirit*. Try to get a clear view of his nature and character, his attributes and his works. Look at the Spirit of the Lord, who first moved over chaos and brought order out of it, and who now visits the chaos of your soul and creates the order of holiness. See him as the Lord and giver of spiritual life, the Illuminator, the Instructor, the Comforter and the Sanctifier. See him as he comes down like holy anointing oil on the head of Jesus, and afterwards rests on *you*, who are like the hem of his robe. If you truly know God, a belief in the Trinity in Unity like this is yours: one you understand, one drawn from Scripture, and one proved in your own experience. And knowing him like that *brings peace indeed*.

modern:
Christ gives his people all the goodness of the past, the present and the future. In the mysterious ages of the past the Lord Jesus was his Father’s first chosen one, and he gave us a share in his *election*, for we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world. From all eternity he had the rights of *Sonship*, as his Father’s only-begotten and dearly loved Son; and in the riches of his grace, by adoption and new birth, he has raised us to sonship too, so that he has given us “power to become the sons of God.” The *eternal covenant*, resting on his pledge to stand guarantor for us and confirmed by an oath, is ours, for our strong comfort and security. In the *everlasting plans of his predestining wisdom* and his all-powerful decree, the eye of the Lord Jesus was always on us; and we can be sure that in the whole scroll of destiny there isn’t one line that works against the good of his redeemed.

The *great engagement* of the Prince of Glory is ours, for it’s to us that he is promised in marriage, as the sacred wedding will soon announce to the whole universe gathered together. The *wonderful incarnation* of the God of heaven is ours, with all the amazing stooping and humbling that came with it. The bloody sweat, the whip, the cross, are ours forever. Whatever blessed results flow from his *perfect obedience, finished atonement, resurrection, ascension or intercession*, they’re all ours by his own gift. On his breastplate he is now carrying our names; and as he pleads with authority at the throne, he remembers us by name and pleads our cause. He uses his *rule* over principalities and powers, and his absolute majesty in heaven, for the good of those who trust in him. His high position is as much at our service as his lowly one was. He who gave himself for us in the depths of grief and death doesn’t take back the gift now that he is enthroned in the highest heavens.

modern:
The church was about to start some hard work, and wanted her Lord’s company in it. She doesn’t say, “I will go,” but “let us go.” Work is a joy when Jesus is at our side! It’s the business of God’s people to tend God’s vines. Like our first parents, we’re put into the Lord’s garden to be useful; so let’s go out into the field.

Notice that the church, when she’s in her right mind, wants to enjoy fellowship with Christ in all her many labors. Some imagine that they can’t serve Christ actively and still have fellowship with him; they’re mistaken. No doubt it’s very easy to fritter away our inner life in outward activity, and end up complaining with the bride, “They made me keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.” But there’s no reason it should be so, except our own foolishness and neglect. It’s certain that a professing Christian can do nothing at all and still grow just as lifeless in spiritual things as the busiest people. Mary wasn’t praised for sitting still, but for *sitting at Jesus’ feet*. In the same way, Christians aren’t to be praised for neglecting their duties on the excuse of having private fellowship with Jesus. It isn’t sitting, but sitting at Jesus’ feet, that deserves praise.

Don’t think that activity is evil in itself; it’s a great blessing, and a means of grace to us. Paul called it a grace given to him to be allowed to preach; and every kind of Christian service can become a personal blessing to those who do it. The people who have most fellowship with Christ aren’t recluses or hermits with lots of time on their hands, but tireless workers who are toiling for Jesus and who, in their toil, have him side by side with them, so that they’re workers together with God. So let’s remember, in anything we have to do for Jesus, that we can do it, and should do it, in close fellowship with him.

modern:
The whole of Christianity rests on the fact that “Christ is risen from the dead”; for “If Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain: ye are yet in your sins.” The *divinity* of Christ finds its surest proof in his resurrection, since he was “Declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead.” It wouldn’t be unreasonable to doubt that he is God if he hadn’t risen. Christ’s *sovereignty* depends on his resurrection too: “For to this end Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and living.” Again, our *justification*, that choice blessing of the covenant, is tied to Christ’s triumphant victory over death and the grave; for “He was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” More than that, our very *new birth* is connected with his resurrection, for we are “Begotten again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” And most certainly our own *final resurrection* rests here, for “If the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.”

If Christ isn’t risen, then we won’t rise; but if he is risen, then those who are asleep in Christ haven’t perished, but in their flesh will surely see their God. So the silver thread of resurrection runs through all the believer’s blessings, from his new birth on to his eternal glory, and ties them together. How important this glorious fact will be to him, then, and how he’ll rejoice that it’s established beyond a doubt that “now is Christ risen from the dead.”

modern:
Believer, you can testify that Christ is *the only begotten of the Father*, as well as the firstborn from the dead. You can say, “He is divine to me, even if he’s only human to the rest of the world. He has done for me what no one but God could do. He has subdued my stubborn will, melted a heart as hard as diamond, opened gates of bronze and snapped bars of iron. He has turned my mourning into laughter and my desolation into joy; he has led my captivity captive, and made my heart rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. Let others think what they like of him; to me he must be the only begotten of the Father: blessed be his name.

“And he is *full of grace*. Ah, if he hadn’t been, I’d never have been saved. He drew me when I struggled to escape from his grace; and when at last I came, all trembling like a condemned criminal, to his mercy-seat, he said, ‘Thy sins which are many are all forgiven thee: be of good cheer.’

“And he is *full of truth*. His promises have been true; not one has failed. I can testify that no servant ever had such a master as I have; no brother ever had such a kinsman as he has been to me; no bride ever had such a husband as Christ has been to my soul; no sinner ever had a better Savior; no mourner ever had a better comforter than Christ has been to my spirit. I want no one but him. In life he is my life, and in death he’ll be the death of death. In poverty Christ is my riches; in sickness he makes my bed; in darkness he is my star, and in brightness he is my sun. He is the manna of the camp in the wilderness, and he’ll be the new grain of the army when they come to Canaan. To me Jesus is all grace and no anger, all truth and no falsehood; and he is *full* of truth and grace, infinitely full. My soul, tonight, bless ‘the only Begotten’ with all your might.”

modern:
It’s good that there is One who is always the same, and who is always with us. It’s good that there is one steady rock among the waves of the sea of life. My soul, don’t set your heart on treasures that rust, that moths eat, that decay; set your heart on him who stays faithful to you forever. Don’t build your house on the shifting quicksands of a deceitful world; build your hopes on this rock, which will stand immovably secure through pouring rain and roaring floods. My soul, I command you: store your treasure in the only safe cabinet; keep your jewels where you can never lose them. Put your all in Christ. Set all your affections on his person, all your hope in his merit, all your trust in his powerful blood, all your joy in his presence; and then you can laugh at loss and defy destruction.

Remember that all the flowers in the world’s garden fade one by one, and the day is coming when nothing will be left but the black, cold earth. Death’s black snuffer must soon put out your candle. Oh, how sweet to have sunlight when the candle is gone! The dark flood must soon roll between you and everything you have; so wed your heart to him who will never leave you. Trust yourself to him who will go with you through the black, surging current of death’s stream, who will land you safely on the heavenly shore and seat you with him in heavenly places forever. Go, grieving child of sorrow, tell your secrets to the Friend who sticks closer than a brother. Trust all your concerns to him who can never be taken from you, who will never leave you, and who will never let you leave him: “Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.” “Lo, I am with you alway” is enough for my soul to live on, whoever else may forsake me.

modern:
Our God’s tender love for his servants makes him care about how they feel inside. He wants them to be of good courage. Some think it’s a small thing for a believer to be troubled by doubts and fears, but God doesn’t think so. This text makes it plain that our Master doesn’t want us tangled up in fears. He’d have us free of anxiety, free of doubt, free of cowardice. Our Master doesn’t think as lightly of our unbelief as we do. When we’re downhearted we have a serious illness, not something to play with, but something to be taken at once to the beloved Physician. Our Lord doesn’t like to see our faces sad. Ahasuerus had a law that no one could come into the king’s court dressed in mourning. That isn’t the law of the King of kings, for we may come mourning just as we are; but still he’d have us take off the spirit of heaviness and put on the garment of praise, for there’s plenty of reason to rejoice.

The Christian ought to have a courageous spirit, so that he may glorify the Lord by bearing trials heroically. If he is fearful and fainthearted, *it will dishonor his God*. Besides, *what a bad example it is*. This disease of doubt and discouragement is an epidemic that soon spreads through the Lord’s flock. One downcast believer makes twenty souls sad. What’s more, unless you keep your courage up, *Satan will be too much for you*. Let your spirit be joyful in God your Savior; the joy of the Lord will be your strength, and no fiend of hell will make headway against you. But cowardice throws down the flag. Again, *work is light* to someone with a cheerful spirit, and *success follows cheerfulness*. The man who toils rejoicing in his God, believing with all his heart, has success guaranteed. He who sows in hope will reap in joy; so, dear reader, “be thou strong, and very courageous.”

modern:
The Lord Jesus gives special revelations of himself to his people. Even if Scripture didn’t say so, there are many of God’s children who could testify to it from their own experience. They have had their Lord and Savior Jesus Christ show himself to them in a special way, such as no mere reading or hearing could give. In the life stories of eminent saints you’ll find many cases where Jesus has been pleased, in a very special way, to speak to their souls and unfold the wonders of his person. Yes, their souls have been so steeped in happiness that they thought they were in heaven, when they weren’t there, though they were very nearly on its doorstep; for when Jesus shows himself to his people, it’s heaven on earth, it’s paradise in seed form, it’s bliss begun.

These special showings of Christ have a holy influence on the believer’s heart. One effect will be *humility*. If someone says, “I have had such-and-such spiritual communications, I am a great man,” he has never had any fellowship with Jesus at all; for “God hath respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth *afar off*.” He doesn’t need to come near them to know them, and he’ll never pay them any visits of love. Another effect will be *happiness*; for in God’s presence there are pleasures forevermore. *Holiness* is sure to follow too. A man who has no holiness has never had this showing. Some people claim a great deal; but we mustn’t believe anyone unless we see that his deeds match what he says. “Be not deceived; God is not mocked.” He won’t give his favors to the wicked; for while he won’t throw away a blameless man, he won’t support an evildoer either. So nearness to Jesus will have three effects: humility, happiness and holiness. May God give them to you, Christian!

modern:
Jacob must have shuddered at the thought of leaving the land where his father had lived, to live among foreign pagans. It was *a new scene, and likely to be a trying one*: who could go among the courtiers of a foreign king without anxiety? Yet the way was *clearly appointed* for him, and so he made up his mind to go. Believers are often in this position now: they’re called into dangers and temptations they’ve never faced before. At such times *let them follow Jacob’s example*, offering sacrifices of prayer to God and seeking his guidance. Let them not take a step until they’ve waited on the Lord for his blessing; then they *will have Jacob’s companion* as their friend and helper. How blessed to feel sure that the Lord is with us in all our ways, and stoops to go down with us into our humiliations and exiles! Even beyond the ocean our Father’s love shines like the sun in its strength. We can’t hesitate to go where Jehovah promises his presence; even the valley of the shadow of death grows bright with the glow of this assurance.

Marching on with faith in their God, believers *will have Jacob’s promise*. They’ll be brought up again, whether from the troubles of life or the chambers of death. Jacob’s descendants came out of Egypt in due time, and so all the faithful will pass unharmed through the trouble of life and the terror of death. Let’s *share Jacob’s confidence*. “Fear not” is the Lord’s command, and his divine encouragement to those who are setting out on new seas at his bidding; the divine presence and protection rule out even one unbelieving fear. Without our God we’d be afraid to move; but when he tells us to go, it would be dangerous to stay. Reader, go forward, and don’t be afraid.

Our trials will seem light and momentary afflictions then. Let’s go on boldly; however dark the night, the morning is coming, which is more than those shut up in the darkness of hell can say. modern:
Look at your possessions, believer, and compare your portion with what other people have. Some have their portion in the field: they’re rich, and their harvests bring them a golden profit. But what are harvests compared with your God, who is the God of harvests? What are bursting barns compared with him, who is the Farmer and feeds you with the bread of heaven? Some have their portion in the city: their wealth is huge and flows to them in constant streams, until they become a reservoir of gold. But what is gold compared with your God? You couldn’t live on it; your spiritual life couldn’t be kept going by it. Lay it on a troubled conscience: could it ease its pain? Put it to a downcast heart: could it stop a single groan, or take away a single grief? But you have God, and in him you have more than gold or riches could ever buy.

Some have their portion in what most people love, applause and fame. But ask yourself, isn’t your God more to you than that? What if countless trumpets blared your praise: would that prepare you to cross the Jordan, or cheer you as you face the judgment? No, there are griefs in life that wealth can’t ease; and there is the deep need of the hour of death, which no riches can provide for. But when you have *God* as your portion, you have more than everything else put together. In him every need is met, whether in life or in death. With God as your portion you’re rich indeed, for he will supply your needs, comfort your heart, soothe your grief, guide your steps, be with you in the dark valley, and then take you home to enjoy him as your portion forever. “I have enough,” said Esau; that’s the best a worldly man can say. But Jacob replies, “I have all things,” which is a note too high for minds set on this world.

modern:
The boundless realms of his Father’s universe belong to Christ by long-established right. As “heir of all things,” he is the sole owner of God’s vast creation; and he has allowed us to claim the whole of it as ours, by the deed of joint heirship that the Lord has signed and sealed with his chosen people. The golden streets of paradise, the pearly gates, the river of life, the surpassing bliss and the glory beyond words have all been signed over to us by our blessed Lord, to own forever. Everything he has, he shares with his people. He has placed the royal crown on the head of his church, appointing her a kingdom and calling her sons a royal priesthood, a race of priests and kings. He took off his own crown so that we might be crowned with glory; he wouldn’t sit on his own throne until he had won a place on it for all who overcome by his blood. Crown the head, and the whole body shares the honor.

See here the reward of every Christian conqueror! Christ’s throne, crown, scepter, palace, treasure, robes and inheritance are yours. Far above the jealousy, selfishness and greed that won’t let anyone share their advantages, Christ counts his happiness complete only when his people share it. “The glory which thou gavest me have I given them.” “These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.” His Father’s smiles are all the sweeter to him because his people share them. The honors of his kingdom please him more because his people appear with him in glory. His conquests are more precious to him because they have taught his people to overcome. He delights in his throne because there is a place on it for them. He rejoices in his royal robes because he spreads their hem over his people. He delights all the more in his joy because he calls them to enter into it.

modern: Who is it that these gracious words are spoken about? He is *the Good Shepherd*. *Why* does he carry the lambs close to his heart? Because *he has a tender heart, and any weakness melts it at once*. The sighs, the ignorance, the weakness of the little ones of his flock call out his compassion. *It’s his duty*, as a faithful High Priest, to care for the weak. Besides, *he bought them with blood; they’re his property*: he must and will care for what cost him so dearly. Then he is *responsible for each lamb*, bound by the terms of the covenant not to lose one. What’s more, *they’re all part of his glory and reward*.

But how should we understand the words “He will *carry* them”? Sometimes he carries them by *not letting them suffer much trial*. Providence deals gently with them. Often they’re “carried” by being filled with *an unusual degree of love*, so that they hold up and stand firm. Their knowledge may not be deep, but they find great sweetness in what they do know. Often he “carries” them by giving them *a very simple faith*, which takes the promise just as it stands and, believing, runs with every trouble straight to Jesus. The simplicity of their faith gives them unusual confidence, which carries them above the world.

“He carries the lambs *in his bosom*.” Here is *boundless love*. Would he hold them to his heart if he didn’t love them very much? Here is *tender nearness*: they’re so near that they couldn’t possibly be nearer. Here is *holy closeness*: there are precious exchanges of love between Christ and his weak ones. Here is *perfect safety*: held to his heart, who can hurt them? They’d have to hurt the Shepherd first. Here is *perfect rest and sweetest comfort*. Surely we don’t feel nearly enough how infinitely tender Jesus is!

modern:
Whoever believes in Christ receives a *present* justification. Faith doesn’t produce this fruit by and by, but *now*. As far as justification is the result of faith, it’s given to the soul the moment it takes hold of Christ and accepts him as its all in all. Are those who stand before God’s throne justified now? So are we, just as truly and clearly justified as those who walk in white and sing sweet praises to heavenly harps. The thief on the cross was justified the moment he turned the eye of faith to Jesus; and Paul the aged, after years of service, was no more justified than the thief was with no service at all. We are *today* accepted in the Beloved, *today* absolved from sin, *today* acquitted at God’s bar of judgment. Oh, what a thought to carry the soul away!

There are some clusters of Eshcol’s vine that we won’t be able to gather until we enter heaven; but this is a branch that runs over the wall. This isn’t like the grain of the land, which we can never eat until we cross the Jordan; this is part of the manna in the wilderness, a share of the daily food God supplies us with on our journey to and fro. We are pardoned *now*, even *now*; even *now* our sins are put away; even *now* we stand accepted in God’s sight, as though we had never been guilty. “There is therefore *now* no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” There isn’t a single sin in God’s book, even *now*, against one of his people. Who dares to bring any charge against them? There’s no speck or spot or wrinkle or any such thing left on a single believer, as far as justification goes, in the sight of the Judge of all the earth. Let our present privilege wake us up to our present duty; and now, while life lasts, let’s spend and be spent for our sweet Lord Jesus.

modern:
Remember that there are two kinds of perfection the Christian needs: the perfection of justification in the person of Jesus, and the perfection of sanctification worked in him by the Holy Spirit. For now, corruption still remains even in the hearts of the born again; experience soon teaches us that. There are still evil desires and evil imaginings inside us. But I rejoice to know that the day is coming when God will finish the work he has begun; and he will present my soul not only perfect in Christ, but perfect through the Spirit, without spot or blemish or any such thing. Can it be true that this poor sinful heart of mine is to become holy, just as God is holy? Can it be that this spirit, which so often cries, “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this sin and death?” will get rid of sin and death, that I’ll have no evil things to trouble my ears and no unholy thoughts to disturb my peace? Oh, happy hour! May it come quickly!

When I cross the Jordan, the work of sanctification will be finished; but not until that moment will I claim perfection in myself at all. Then my spirit will have its last baptism in the Holy Spirit’s fire. I think I long to die to receive that last and final cleansing which will bring me into heaven. No angel will be purer than I’ll be, for I’ll be able to say in a double sense, “I am clean”: through Jesus’ blood, and through the Spirit’s work. Oh, how we should praise the power of the Holy Spirit for making us fit, like this, to stand before our Father in heaven!

Yet don’t let the hope of perfection later make us content with imperfection now. If it does, our hope can’t be genuine; for a good hope makes us pure, even now. The work of grace must be *living in us now*, or it can’t be *perfected then*. Let’s pray to “be filled with the Spirit,” so that we may bear the fruits of righteousness *more and more*.

modern:
Our Lord Jesus is always giving, and never for a single moment draws back his hand. As long as there’s a vessel of grace not yet full to the brim, the oil won’t stop flowing. He is a sun that’s always shining; he is manna always falling around the camp; he is a rock in the desert, always sending out streams of life from his struck side. The rain of his grace is always falling, the river of his generosity is always flowing, and the spring of his love is constantly overflowing. As the King can never die, so his grace can never fail. Every day we pick his fruit, and every day his branches bend down to our hand with a fresh supply of mercy. There are seven feast days in his weeks, and as many banquets in his years as there are days. Who has ever come back from his door without a blessing? Who has ever got up from his table unsatisfied, or from his embrace without finding paradise? His mercies are new every morning and fresh every evening.

Who can know the number of his benefits, or list all his gifts? Every grain of sand that drops from the hourglass of time only trails slowly behind countless mercies. The wings of our hours are covered with the silver of his kindness and the yellow gold of his affection. The river of time carries down the golden sands of his favor from the mountains of eternity. The countless stars are only the flag-bearers of an even more countless army of blessings. Who can count the dust of the benefits he gives to Jacob, or number the fourth part of his mercies toward Israel? How shall my soul praise him who daily loads us with benefits and crowns us with loving-kindness? Oh, that my praise could be as unending as his generosity! Miserable tongue, how can you be silent? Wake up, I beg you, or I’ll call you no longer my glory, but my shame. “Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake right early.”

modern:
The armies of the three kings were dying of thirst. God was about to send water, and in these words the prophet announced the coming blessing. Here was *a case of human helplessness*: all their brave men together couldn’t get a drop of water from the skies or find one in the wells of the earth. The Lord’s people are often at their wits’ end like this; they see how empty created things are, and learn by experience where their help is to be found. Still, the people were to make *a believing preparation for the divine blessing*: they were to dig the trenches that would hold the precious water. The church must make herself ready to be blessed through all her various works, efforts and prayers; she must make the pools, and the Lord will fill them. This must be done in faith, fully sure that the blessing is about to come down.

By and by there was *an unusual giving of the gift they needed*. The shower didn’t pour from the clouds as it did for Elijah; the pools were filled in a silent and mysterious way. The Lord has his own sovereign ways of working: he isn’t tied to times and methods as we are, but does as he pleases among the sons of men. Our part is to receive from him thankfully, not to dictate to him. We must also notice *the remarkable abundance of the supply*: there was enough for everyone’s need. And so it is with the blessing of the gospel. All the needs of the congregation and of the whole church will be met by the divine power in answer to prayer; and on top of all this, the armies of the Lord will soon be given victory.
What am I doing for Jesus? What trenches am I digging? O Lord, make me ready to receive the blessing you are so willing to give.

modern:
Why should Christians imitate Christ? They should do it *for their own sakes*. If they want to be in a healthy state of soul, if they would escape the sickness of sin and enjoy the strength of growing grace, let Jesus be their model. For the sake of their own happiness, if they would drink the finest aged wine, well refined; if they would enjoy holy and happy fellowship with Jesus; if they would be lifted up above the cares and troubles of this world, let them walk just as he walked. Nothing can help you travel toward heaven with good speed like wearing the image of Jesus on your heart to rule all its movements. It’s when, by the power of the Holy Spirit, you’re able to walk with Jesus in his very footsteps that you’re happiest, and most plainly seen to be sons of God. Peter following at a distance is both unsafe and uneasy.

Next, strive to be like Jesus *for religion’s sake*. Ah, poor religion, you’ve been badly shot at by cruel enemies, but you haven’t been wounded half so dangerously by your enemies as by your friends. Who made those wounds in the fair hand of godliness? The professing Christian who used the dagger of hypocrisy. The man who gets into the fold under false pretenses, nothing but a wolf in sheep’s clothing, worries the flock more than the lion outside. There’s no weapon half so deadly as a Judas kiss. Inconsistent professing Christians harm the gospel more than the sneering critic or the unbeliever.

But above all, imitate his example *for Christ’s own sake*. Christian, do you love your Savior? Is his name precious to you? Is his cause dear to you? Would you like to see the kingdoms of the world become his? Do you want him to be glorified? Are you longing for souls to be won to him? If so, *imitate* Jesus; be an “epistle of Christ, known and read of all men.”

modern:
If we have received the grace of God in our hearts, its practical effect has been to make us God’s *servants*. We may be unfaithful servants, and we’re certainly unprofitable ones, but still, blessed be his name, we *are* his servants: we wear his uniform, eat at his table and obey his commands. We were once the servants of sin, but he who set us free has now taken us into his family and taught us to obey his will. We don’t serve our Master perfectly, but we would if we could. As we hear God’s voice saying to us, “Thou art my servant,” we can answer with David, “I am thy servant; thou hast loosed my bonds.”

But the Lord calls us not only his *servants*, but his *chosen* ones: “I have chosen thee.” We didn’t choose him first; he chose us. If we are God’s servants, we weren’t always so; the change must be credited to sovereign grace. The eye of sovereignty picked us out, and the voice of unchanging grace declared, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love.” Long before time began or space was made, God had written the names of his chosen people on his heart, had predestined them to be shaped into the likeness of his Son, and appointed them heirs of all the fullness of his love, his grace and his glory.

What comfort there is here! Has the Lord loved us so long, and will he throw us away now? He knew how stubborn we’d be; he understood that our hearts were evil; and still he made his choice. Ah, our Savior is no fickle lover. He isn’t charmed for a while by a few gleams of beauty in his church’s eye, only to cast her off later because she is unfaithful. No, he married her in eternity past; and it’s written of Jehovah, “He hateth putting away.” The eternal choice is a bond on *our* gratitude and on *his* faithfulness, which neither can disown.

modern:
All the attributes of Christ, as God and man, are at our disposal. All the fullness of the Godhead, whatever that wonderful phrase may include, is ours to make us complete. He can’t give us the attributes of God himself; but he has done all that can be done, for he has made even his divine power and Godhead serve our salvation. His being all-powerful, all-knowing and present everywhere, his unchangeableness and his inability to err, are all joined together to defend us. Get up, believer, and see the Lord Jesus harnessing the whole of his divine Godhead to the chariot of salvation! How vast his grace, how firm his faithfulness, how unswerving his unchangeableness, how infinite his power, how limitless his knowledge! The Lord Jesus has made all these the pillars of the temple of salvation; and all of them, without the least shrinking of their infinity, are promised to us by covenant as our everlasting inheritance.

Every drop of the bottomless love of the Savior’s heart is ours. Every muscle in the arm of might, every jewel in the crown of majesty, the vastness of divine knowledge and the sternness of divine justice: all are ours, and will be used for us. The whole of Christ, in his adorable character as the Son of God, he himself has signed over to us for us to enjoy to the full. His wisdom is our guidance, his knowledge our teaching, his power our protection, his justice our guarantee, his love our comfort, his mercy our consolation, and his unchangeableness our trust. He holds nothing back, but opens the depths of the Mount of God and tells us to dig in its mines for the hidden treasures. “All, all, all are yours,” he says, “be ye satisfied with favour and full of the goodness of the Lord.” Oh, how sweet to see Jesus like this, and to call on him with complete confidence that when we ask his love or power to step in for us, we’re only asking for what he has already faithfully promised.

modern:
How happy tried Christians are *afterward*! There’s no calm deeper than the one that follows a storm. Who hasn’t rejoiced in clear sunshine after rain? Victory banquets are for battle-hardened soldiers. After killing the lion we eat the honey; after climbing the Hill Difficulty, we sit down in the arbor to rest; after crossing the Valley of Humiliation, after fighting with Apollyon, the shining one appears with the healing branch from the tree of life. Our sorrows, like the keels of ships passing over the sea, leave a silver line of holy light behind them “afterwards.” It’s peace, sweet, deep peace, that follows the horrible turmoil that once ruled in our tormented, guilty souls.

See, then, how happy the Christian’s condition is! He has his best things last, and so in this world he gets his worst things first. But even his worst things are good things “afterward”: harsh plowings that yield joyful harvests. Even now he grows rich by his losses, he rises by his falls, he lives by dying, and becomes full by being emptied. If his painful troubles yield him so much peaceable fruit in this life, then, what will the full harvest of joy be “afterwards” in heaven? If his dark nights are as bright as the world’s days, what will his days be? If even his starlight is more splendid than the sun, what must his sunlight be? If he can sing in a dungeon, how sweetly he’ll sing in heaven! If he can praise the Lord in the fires, how he’ll extol him before the eternal throne! If evil is good to him *now*, what will the overflowing goodness of God be to him *then*? Oh, blessed “afterward”! Who wouldn’t be a Christian? Who wouldn’t bear the present cross for the crown that comes afterward? But here is work for patience, for the rest isn’t for today, nor the triumph for now, but “afterward.” Wait, my soul, and let patience have her perfect work.

modern: Upstarts often grab the highest places, while the truly great waste away unnoticed. This is a riddle of providence, and its answer will one day gladden the hearts of the upright; but it happens so often that none of us should grumble if it falls to our own lot. When our Lord was on earth, though he is the Prince of the kings of the earth, he walked the footpath of weariness and service as the Servant of servants. So is it any wonder if his followers, who are princes of royal blood, are also looked down on as inferior and contemptible people? The world is upside down, and so the first are last and the last first. See how the slavish sons of Satan lord it over the earth! What a high horse they ride! How they lift up their horn on high! Haman is at court, while Mordecai sits in the gate; David wanders on the mountains, while Saul reigns in state; Elijah is complaining in the cave, while Jezebel is boasting in the palace. Yet who would want to take the places of the proud rebels? And who, on the other hand, wouldn’t envy the despised saints? When the wheel turns, those who are lowest rise, and the highest sink. Patience, then, believer: eternity will right the wrongs of time.

Let’s not make the mistake of letting our passions and bodily appetites ride in triumph while our nobler powers walk in the dust. Grace must reign as a prince, and make the members of the body instruments of righteousness. The Holy Spirit loves order, and so he sets our powers and faculties in their proper rank and place, giving the highest place to the spiritual faculties that link us with the great King. Let’s not upset the divine arrangement, but ask for grace to keep our body under and bring it into subjection. We weren’t created anew so that our passions could rule over us, but so that we, as kings, may reign in Christ Jesus over the threefold kingdom of spirit, soul and body, to the glory of God the Father.

modern:
It was a remarkable thing that the man who was never to die, for whom God had appointed an infinitely better lot, the man who would be carried to heaven in a chariot of fire and taken up without seeing death, should pray like this: “Let me die, I am no better than my fathers.” Here we have a memorable proof that God doesn’t always answer prayer in kind, though he always does in effect. He gave Elijah something better than what he asked for, and so really heard him and answered him. It was strange that lion-hearted Elijah should be so cast down by Jezebel’s threat that he asked to die; and it was blessedly kind of our heavenly Father not to take his despairing servant at his word.

There’s a limit to the teaching about the prayer of faith. We aren’t to expect that God will give us everything we choose to ask for. We know that we sometimes ask and don’t receive, because we ask wrongly. If we ask for something that isn’t promised; if we go against the spirit the Lord wants us to grow in; if we ask against his will or the plans of his providence; if we ask only to make ourselves comfortable, with no eye to his glory, we mustn’t expect to receive. Yet when we ask in faith, not doubting at all, then even if we don’t receive the exact thing we asked for, we’ll receive something just as good, and better than just as good. As someone has said, “If the Lord does not pay in silver, he will in gold; and if he does not pay in gold, he will in diamonds.” If he doesn’t give you exactly what you ask for, he’ll give you something equal to it, something you’ll be very glad to receive instead. So, dear reader, pray much, and make this evening a time of earnest intercession; but be careful what you ask for.

modern:
When we give our hearts along with our gifts to the poor, we give well; but we often have to plead guilty to failing in this. Not so our Master and our Lord. His favors are always done with the love of his heart. He doesn’t send us the cold meat and leftover scraps from his rich table; he dips our piece of bread in his own dish, and seasons our food with the spices of his fragrant affection. When he puts the golden tokens of his grace into our palms, he gives the gift with such a warm squeeze of our hand that the way he gives is as precious as the gift itself. He comes into our houses on his errands of kindness, and he doesn’t act the way some stern visitors do in a poor man’s cottage; he sits by our side, not looking down on our poverty or blaming our weakness. Dear friend, with what smiles he speaks! What golden words drop from his gracious lips! What embraces of love he gives us!

If he had given us only pennies, the way he gave them would have turned them to gold; but as it is, his pleasant manner sets his costly gifts in a golden basket. It’s impossible to doubt that his kindness is sincere, for a bleeding heart is stamped on the face of all his gifts. He gives generously and doesn’t scold. Not one hint that we’re a burden to him; not one cold look for the poor people who live on his charity. He rejoices in his mercy, and holds us close to his heart while he is pouring out his life for us. There’s a fragrance in his perfume that nothing but his heart could produce; there’s a sweetness in his honeycomb that couldn’t be there unless the very essence of his soul’s love had been mixed into it. Oh, the rare fellowship that such unusual warmth brings about! May we always taste and know how blessed it is!

modern:
Our heavenly Father often draws us with the cords of love; but ah, how slow we are to run to him! How slowly we respond to his gentle urging! *He draws us to a simpler faith in him*; but we haven’t yet reached Abraham’s confidence. We don’t leave our worldly cares with God, but like Martha, we weigh ourselves down with much serving. Our thin faith makes our souls thin; we don’t open our mouths wide, though God has promised to fill them. Isn’t he drawing us to trust him this evening? Can’t we hear him say, “Come, my child, and trust me. The veil is torn; come into my presence, and approach the throne of my grace boldly. I’m worthy of your fullest confidence; throw your cares on me. Shake off the dust of your cares, and put on your beautiful clothes of joy”? But sadly, though we’re called with tones of love to this blessed, comforting grace, we won’t come.

At other times *he draws us to closer fellowship with himself*. We’ve been sitting on the doorstep of God’s house, and he tells us to come on into the banquet hall and eat with him; but we decline the honor. There are secret rooms not yet opened to us; Jesus invites us to go in, but we hold back. Shame on our cold hearts! We’re poor lovers of our sweet Lord Jesus, not fit to be his servants, much less his bride; and yet he has raised us to be bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh, married to him by a glorious marriage covenant. Here is love! But it’s love that *won’t take no for an answer*. If we don’t obey the gentle drawing of his love, he’ll send trouble to drive us into closer friendship with himself. He will have us nearer. What foolish children we are to refuse those bands of love, and so bring on our backs that whip of small cords that Jesus knows how to use!

modern: *If*: then this isn’t something to be taken for granted about every member of the human race. “*If*”: then it’s possible, even likely, that some haven’t tasted that the Lord is gracious. “*If*”: then this isn’t a general mercy but a special one, and we need to ask whether we know the grace of God by inner experience. There’s no spiritual favor that can’t be a matter for searching our hearts.

But while this should be a matter of earnest and prayerful inquiry, no one ought to be content while there’s any “if” at all about his having tasted that the Lord is gracious. A jealous and holy distrust of self may raise the question even in a believer’s heart, but for such a doubt to *go on* would be an evil indeed. We mustn’t rest without a desperate struggle to clasp the Savior in the arms of faith and say, “I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him.” Believer, don’t rest until you’re fully sure that you have a share in Jesus. Let nothing satisfy you until the Holy Spirit, who can’t be wrong, bears witness with your spirit and assures you that you’re a child of God. Oh, don’t play games here; don’t let any “perhaps” or “possibly” or “if” or “maybe” satisfy your soul. Build on eternal truths, and build on them truly. Get the sure mercies of David, and get them surely. Let your anchor be cast into what lies behind the veil, and make sure your soul is tied to the anchor by a cable that won’t break. Get past these dreary “ifs”; stay no longer in the wilderness of doubts and fears; cross the Jordan of distrust and enter the Canaan of peace, where the Canaanite still lingers, but where the land never stops flowing with milk and honey.

modern:
Famine gripped all the nations, and it seemed certain that Jacob and his family would suffer great want. But the God of providence, who never forgets those he has chosen to love, had stocked a granary for his people. He had warned the Egyptians of the famine and led them to store up the grain of the years of plenty. Jacob little expected rescue from Egypt, but there was the grain, stored up for him.

Believer, though everything seems to be against you, rest assured that God has set something aside for you; in the list of your griefs there’s a saving clause. Somehow he’ll rescue you, and somewhere he’ll provide for you. Your rescue may come from a very unexpected direction, but help will surely come in your hour of greatest need, and you’ll praise the name of the Lord. If people don’t feed you, ravens will; and if the earth doesn’t yield wheat, heaven will drop manna. So be of good courage, and rest quietly in the Lord. God can make the sun rise in the west if he pleases, and turn the source of distress into the channel of delight.

The grain in Egypt was all in the hands of Joseph, the beloved son; he opened or closed the granaries as he chose. In the same way all the riches of providence are in the absolute power of our Lord Jesus, who will hand them out generously to his people. Joseph was more than ready to help his own family; and Jesus never stops caring faithfully for his brothers. Our business is to go after the help provided for us. We mustn’t sit still in despair, but stir ourselves. Prayer will soon carry us into the presence of our royal Brother. Once before his throne we have only to ask and have. His storehouses aren’t empty; there’s still grain. His heart isn’t hard; he’ll give the grain to us. Lord, forgive our unbelief, and this evening move us to draw freely from your fullness and receive grace upon grace.

modern:
Changing experiences often lead the anxious believer to ask, “Why is it thus with me?” I looked for light, but look, darkness came; for peace, but trouble came instead. I said in my heart, my mountain stands firm, I’ll never be moved. Lord, you hide your face, and I’m troubled. Only yesterday I could read my title to heaven clearly; today my evidences are dimmed and my hopes are clouded. Yesterday I could climb to the top of Pisgah and look out over the landscape, and rejoice with confidence in my future inheritance; today my spirit has no hopes but many fears, no joys but much distress. Is this part of God’s plan for me? Can this be the way God would bring me to heaven?

Yes, it is. The eclipse of your faith, the darkness of your mind, the fainting of your hope: all these things are only parts of God’s method of making you ripe for the great inheritance you’ll soon enter. These trials are for the testing and strengthening of your faith. They’re waves that wash you farther up onto the rock; they’re winds that carry your ship all the faster toward the haven you long for. As David says, so it may be said of you: “so he bringeth them to their desired haven.” By honor and dishonor, by bad report and good report, by plenty and by poverty, by joy and by distress, by persecution and by peace: by all these things the life of your soul is kept going, and by each of them you’re helped on your way. Oh, don’t think, believer, that your sorrows are outside God’s plan; they’re necessary parts of it. “We must, through much tribulation, enter the kingdom.” Learn, then, even to “count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations.”

modern:
From every angle our Beloved is beautiful. Our heavenly Father means our various experiences to give us fresh viewpoints from which to see the loveliness of Jesus. How lovely our trials are when they carry us up high, where we can get clearer views of Jesus than ordinary life could give us! We have seen him from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, and he has shone on us like the sun in its strength; but we have also seen him “from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards,” and he has lost none of his loveliness. From the weakness of a sickbed, from the edge of the grave, we have turned our eyes to our soul’s husband, and he has never been anything but “all fair.” Many of his saints have looked at him from the gloom of dungeons and the red flames of the stake, yet they have never said a bad word about him, but have died praising his surpassing beauty.

Oh, what a noble and pleasant occupation, to be forever gazing at our sweet Lord Jesus! Isn’t it delightful beyond words to see the Savior in all his offices, and to find him matchless in each one: to turn the kaleidoscope, so to speak, and find fresh patterns of unequaled graces? In the manger and in eternity, on the cross and on his throne, in the garden and in his kingdom, among thieves or among cherubim, he is everywhere “altogether lovely.” Examine carefully every little act of his life and every trait of his character, and he is as lovely in the smallest things as in the greatest. Judge him however you like, you can’t find fault; weigh him however you please, and he won’t be found wanting. Eternity won’t discover the shadow of a spot in our Beloved; rather, as the ages roll on, his hidden glories will shine out with still more unimaginable splendor, and his indescribable loveliness will more and more enrapture every mind in heaven.

modern:
Very clearly, the confidence the psalmist expressed here was a *divine confidence*. He didn’t say, “*I* have grace enough to perfect what concerns me. My faith is so steady that it won’t stagger; my love is so warm that it will never grow cold; my resolve is so firm that nothing can move it.” No, his dependence was on the Lord alone. If we indulge in any confidence that isn’t grounded on the Rock of Ages, our confidence is worse than a dream: it will fall on us and bury us in its ruins, to our sorrow and shame. Everything nature spins, time will unravel, to the eternal shame of all who are clothed in it. The psalmist was wise; he rested on nothing short of the *Lord’s* work. It’s the Lord who began the good work in us; it’s he who has carried it on; and if he doesn’t finish it, it will never be complete. If there’s one stitch in the heavenly robe of our righteousness that we have to put in ourselves, then we’re lost; but this is our confidence: the Lord who began will perfect it. He *has* done it all, *must* do it all, and *will* do it all. Our confidence mustn’t be in what we have done, nor in what we have resolved to do, but entirely in what *the Lord* will do.

Unbelief whispers, “You’ll never be able to stand. Look at the evil in your heart; you can never conquer sin. Remember the sinful pleasures and temptations of the world all around you; you’ll certainly be lured by them and led astray.” Ah, yes, we really would perish if we were left to our own strength. If we had to steer our fragile boats across so rough a sea alone, we might well give up the voyage in despair. But thanks be to God, he will perfect what concerns us, and bring us to the haven we long for. We can never be too confident when we trust in him alone, and never too concerned to *have* a trust like that.
