modern:
Worshipers at the temple used to bring gifts of sweet perfume to be burned on God’s altar. But Israel, in her backsliding days, grew stingy and brought her Lord very few freewill offerings; and this showed how cold her heart had grown toward God and his house. Reader, does this never happen with you? Couldn’t the complaint of this text be brought against you now and then, if not often? Those who are poor in pocket but rich in faith will be accepted no less because their gifts are small. But, poor reader, do you give the Lord a fair share of what you have, or is the widow’s mite kept back from the sacred treasury? The rich believer should be thankful for the talent entrusted to him, but shouldn’t forget his great responsibility, for where much is given, much will be required. But, rich reader, are you mindful of your obligations, and giving back to the Lord in proportion to what you’ve received? Jesus gave his blood for us; what shall we give to him? We are his, with all we have, for he has bought us for himself. Can we act as if we were our own? Oh, for more dedication! And to that end, oh, for more love!

Blessed Jesus, how good of you to accept our sweet cane bought with money! Nothing is too costly as a tribute to your unrivaled love, and yet you receive with favor the smallest sincere token of affection! You receive our poor forget-me-nots and love tokens as though they were precious in themselves, though really they’re only like the bunch of wildflowers a child brings to its mother. May we never grow stingy toward you, and from this hour may we never hear you complain of us again for holding back the gifts of our love. We’ll give you the firstfruits of our increase and pay you tithes of everything, and then we’ll confess, “of thine own have we given thee.”

modern:
When we look back honestly on the kind of prayers we’ve prayed, we’ll be filled with wonder that God has ever answered them. There may be some who think their prayers deserve to be accepted, as the Pharisee did; but the true Christian, looking back with clearer eyes, weeps over his prayers, and if he could go back over the road, he’d want to pray more earnestly.

Remember, Christian, how *cold* your prayers have been. In your prayer room you should have wrestled as Jacob did; but instead, your requests have been faint and few, far from that humble, believing, persevering faith that cries, “I will not let thee go except thou bless me.” Yet, wonderful to say, God has heard these cold prayers of yours, and not only heard them but answered them. Think too how *seldom* you’ve prayed, except when you were in trouble; *then* you went often to the mercy-seat. But when rescue came, where were your constant requests? Yet though you stopped praying as you once did, God hasn’t stopped blessing. When you neglected the mercy-seat, God didn’t desert it; the bright light of the Shekinah has always been visible between the wings of the cherubim.

Oh, it’s amazing that the Lord should pay attention to those on-and-off fits of urgency that come and go with our needs. What a God he is, to hear the prayers of people who come to him when they’re in pressing need but neglect him once they’ve received a mercy; who come near him when they’re forced to, but almost forget to speak to him when mercies are plentiful and sorrows are few. Let his gracious kindness in hearing prayers like these touch our hearts, so that from now on we may be found “Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit.”

modern:
The word “conversation” doesn’t just mean our talk and chat with one another, but the whole course of our life and behavior in the world. The Greek word means the actions and the privileges of citizenship; so we’re commanded to let our actions, as citizens of the New Jerusalem, be worthy of the gospel of Christ. What kind of conduct is that?

In the first place, *the gospel is very simple*. So Christians should be simple and plain in their habits. There should be in our manner, our speech, our dress, our whole behavior, that simplicity which is the very soul of beauty. The gospel is *above all true*; it’s gold without impurity; and the Christian’s life will be dull and worthless without the jewel of truth. The gospel is a very *fearless gospel*: it boldly proclaims the truth, whether people like it or not; we must be just as faithful and unflinching. But the gospel is also *very gentle*. Notice this spirit in its Founder: “a bruised reed he will not break.” Some professing Christians are pricklier than a thorn hedge; such people aren’t like Jesus. Let’s try to win others by the gentleness of our words and actions. The gospel is *very loving*. It’s the message of the God of love to a lost and fallen race. Christ’s last command to his disciples was, “Love one another.” Oh, for more real, heartfelt unity and love toward all the saints, and for more tender compassion toward the souls of the worst and vilest of people! We mustn’t forget that the gospel of Christ is *holy*. It never excuses sin; it pardons it, but only through an atonement. If our life is to look like the gospel, we must shun not only the grosser vices, but everything that would keep us from becoming perfectly like Christ. For his sake, for our own sakes and for the sake of others, we must strive day by day to make our conduct more and more in keeping with his gospel.

modern:
We often pray that God won’t forsake us in the hour of trial and temptation, but we too easily forget that we need this prayer at *all times*. There’s no moment of our life, however holy, when we can do without his constant upholding. Whether in light or in darkness, in fellowship or in temptation, we need the prayer just the same: “Forsake me not, O Lord.” “Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe.” A little child learning to walk always needs the nurse’s help. A ship left by the pilot drifts off course at once. We can’t do without continual help from above; so let this be your prayer today:

“Don’t forsake me. Father, don’t forsake your child, or he’ll fall by the hand of the enemy. Shepherd, don’t forsake your lamb, or he’ll wander away from the safety of the fold. Great Gardener, don’t forsake your plant, or it will wither and die. ‘Forsake me not, O Lord,’ now; and don’t forsake me at any moment of my life. Don’t forsake me in my joys, or they’ll swallow up my heart. Don’t forsake me in my sorrows, or I’ll grumble against you. Don’t forsake me in the day of my repentance, or I’ll lose the hope of pardon and fall into despair; and don’t forsake me in the day of my strongest faith, or faith will sink into presumption. Don’t forsake me, for without you I’m weak, but with you I’m strong. Don’t forsake me, for my path is dangerous and full of traps, and I can’t do without your guidance. The hen doesn’t forsake her chicks; so always cover me with your feathers, and let me find my refuge under your wings. ‘Be not far from me, O Lord, for trouble is near, for there is none to help.’ ‘Leave me not, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation!’”

modern:
When the two disciples had reached Emmaus and were refreshing themselves with the evening meal, the mysterious stranger who had so captivated them on the road took bread and broke it, made himself known to them, and then vanished from their sight. They had urged him to stay with them because the day was nearly over; but now, though it was much later, their love was a lamp to their feet, and wings too. They forgot the darkness, their tiredness was all gone, and at once they traveled the seven miles back to tell the glad news of a risen Lord who had appeared to them on the way. They reached the Christians in Jerusalem, and were met with a burst of joyful news before they could tell their own story. These early Christians were all on fire to speak of Christ’s resurrection and to proclaim what they knew of the Lord; they shared their experiences as common property.

This evening let their example make a deep impression on us. We too must bear our witness about Jesus. John’s account of the tomb needed Peter’s added to it; and Mary could tell of something more still. Put together, they give us a full testimony that we couldn’t spare any part of. We each have our own special gifts and special showings of Christ; but the one goal God has in view is the perfecting of the whole body of Christ. So we must bring our spiritual possessions and lay them at the apostles’ feet, and share out with everyone what God has given us. Keep back no part of the precious truth, but speak what you know and testify to what you’ve seen. Don’t let the effort, or the darkness, or the possible unbelief of your friends weigh for a moment in the balance. Get up and march to the place of duty, and there tell what great things God has shown your soul.

modern:
Care, even about legitimate things, has something of the nature of sin in it if it’s carried too far. Our Savior earnestly teaches the command to avoid anxious care again and again; the apostles repeat it; and it can’t be ignored without breaking God’s law. For the very essence of anxious care is imagining that we’re wiser than God, and pushing ourselves into his place to do for him what he has undertaken to do for us. We try to think of things we imagine he’ll forget; we struggle to take our weary burden on ourselves, as if he were unable or unwilling to carry it for us. Now this disobedience to his plain command, this unbelief in his Word, this presumption in trespassing on his territory, is all sinful.

More than this, anxious care often leads to sinful actions. Whoever can’t calmly leave his affairs in God’s hand, but insists on carrying his own burden, is very likely to be tempted to use wrong means to help himself. This sin leads us to abandon God as our counselor and turn to human wisdom instead. This is going to the “broken cistern” instead of to the “fountain”: a sin that was charged against Israel long ago. Anxiety makes us doubt God’s loving-kindness, and so our love for him grows cold. We feel mistrust, and so grieve the Spirit of God, so that our prayers are hindered, our consistent example spoiled, and our life becomes one of self-seeking. So a lack of confidence in God leads us to wander far from him. But if through simple faith in his promise we throw each burden on him as it comes, and are “careful for nothing” because he undertakes to care for us, it will keep us close to him and strengthen us against much temptation. “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on thee, because he trusteth in thee.”

modern:
Perseverance is the badge of true saints. The Christian life isn’t just a *beginning* in the ways of God, but also a *continuing* in them as long as life lasts. It’s the same for a Christian as it was for the great Napoleon, who said, “Conquest has made me what I am, and conquest must maintain me.” So, under God, dear friend in the Lord, conquest has made you what you are, and conquest must keep you going. Your motto must be “Excelsior.” The only true conqueror, the one who will be crowned at the last, is the one who keeps on until the trumpet of war is blown no more.

So perseverance is the target of all our spiritual enemies. The *world* doesn’t object to your being a Christian for a while, if only she can tempt you to give up your pilgrimage and settle down to buy and sell with her in Vanity Fair. The *flesh* will try to trap you and stop you from pressing on to glory: “It’s tiring work being a pilgrim; come on, give it up. Am I always to be put to death? Am I never to be indulged? At least give me some leave from this constant war.” *Satan* will make many fierce attacks on your perseverance; it will be the target of all his arrows. He’ll try to hinder you *in service*: he’ll hint that you’re doing no good, and that you need a rest. He’ll try to make you weary of *suffering*; he’ll whisper, “Curse God, and die.” Or he’ll attack your *steadiness*: “What’s the good of being so zealous? Be quiet like everyone else; sleep like the others, and let your lamp go out the way the other virgins do.” Or he’ll attack your *beliefs*: “Why do you hold on to these narrow creeds of your church? Sensible people are getting more broad-minded; they’re moving the old boundary stones. Get in step with the times.” So, Christian, wear your shield close against your armor, and cry out mightily to God, that by his Spirit you may endure to the end.

modern:
Mephibosheth was no great ornament to a royal banquet, yet he had a permanent place at David’s table, because the king could see in his face the features of his beloved friend Jonathan. Like Mephibosheth, we may cry to the King of Glory, “What is thy servant, that thou shouldst look upon such a dead dog as I am?” But still the Lord treats us to the closest friendship with himself, because he sees in our faces the memory of his dearly loved Jesus. The Lord’s people are *dear for another’s sake*. The Father’s love for his only begotten Son is such that, for his sake, he raises his lowly brothers from poverty and exile to the company of the court, to noble rank and royal provision.

Their *deformity won’t rob them of their privileges*. Lameness is no bar to sonship; the cripple is as much the heir as if he could run like Asahel. Our right doesn’t limp, though our strength may. A king’s table is a fine hiding place for lame legs, and at the gospel feast we learn to boast in our weaknesses, because the power of Christ rests on us. Yet *serious disability may disfigure even the best-loved saints*. Here is one who feasted with David, and yet was so lame in both feet that he couldn’t go with the king when he fled from the city, and so was slandered and wronged by his servant Ziba. Saints whose faith is weak and whose knowledge is thin lose a great deal; they’re exposed to many enemies, and can’t follow the King wherever he goes. This *disease often comes from falls*. Bad care in their spiritual infancy often makes converts fall into a discouragement they never recover from, and in other cases sin brings broken bones. Lord, help the lame to leap like a deer, and satisfy all your people with the bread of your table!

modern:
If Mephibosheth was humbled like this by David’s kindness, what will *we* feel in the presence of our gracious Lord? The more grace we have, the less we’ll think of ourselves, for grace, like light, shows up our impurity. Eminent saints have hardly known what to compare themselves to, their sense of unworthiness has been so clear and sharp. “I am,” says holy Rutherford, “a dry and withered branch, a piece of dead carcass, dry bones, and not able to step over a straw.” In another place he writes, “Except as to open outbreakings, I want nothing of what Judas and Cain had.” To a humbled mind, the lowest things in nature seem better than itself, because they have never caught sin. A dog may be greedy, fierce or filthy, but it has no conscience to violate and no Holy Spirit to resist. A dog may be a worthless animal, and yet a little kindness soon wins it to love its master, and it’s faithful to death; but we forget the goodness of the Lord and don’t follow when he calls.

The term “dead dog” is the most expressive of all terms of contempt, but it isn’t too strong to express the self-loathing of believers who have been taught by God. They aren’t putting on false modesty; they mean what they say. They have weighed themselves in the scales of the sanctuary and found out how empty their nature is. At best we’re only clay, dust that breathes, walking mounds of earth; but seen as sinners, we’re monsters indeed. Let it be announced in heaven as a wonder that the Lord Jesus should set his heart’s love on people like us. Dust and ashes though we are, we must and will “magnify the exceeding greatness of his grace.” Couldn’t his heart find rest in heaven? Did he have to come to these tents of Kedar for a wife, and choose a bride darkened by the sun? O heavens and earth, break out into song, and give all glory to our sweet Lord Jesus.

modern: Here’s a precious truth for you, believer. You may be poor, or suffering, or unknown; but for your encouragement, look again at your “calling” and the results that flow from it, and especially the blessed result spoken of here. As surely as you’re God’s child today, so surely will all your trials soon be over, and you’ll be rich in every kind of bliss. Wait a while, and that weary head will wear the crown of glory, and that working hand will grasp the palm branch of victory. Don’t lament your troubles; rather, rejoice that before long you’ll be where “there shall be neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.” The chariots of fire are at your door, and a moment will be enough to carry you to the glorified. The everlasting song is almost on your lips. The gates of heaven stand open for you. Don’t think you can fail to enter into rest. If he has called you, nothing can separate you from his love. Distress can’t cut the bond; the fire of persecution can’t burn the link; the hammer of hell can’t break the chain. You’re secure. The voice that called you at first will call you yet again, from earth to heaven, from death’s dark gloom to the unspoken splendors of immortality. Rest assured, the heart of him who has justified you beats with infinite love toward you. Soon you’ll be with the glorified, where your portion is; you’re only waiting here to be made fit for the inheritance, and once that’s done, the wings of angels will carry you far away to the mountain of peace and joy and blessedness, where,
you’ll rest forever and ever.

modern:
Memory is often the slave of despondency. Despairing minds call to mind every dark foreboding of the past, and dwell at length on every gloomy feature of the present; so memory, dressed in sackcloth, hands the mind a cup mixed with gall and wormwood. There’s no need for this, though. Wisdom can easily turn memory into an angel of comfort. The same remembering that brings so many gloomy omens in its left hand can be trained to carry a wealth of hopeful signs in its right. She doesn’t have to wear a crown of iron; she can circle her forehead with a band of gold, all spangled with stars.

So it was in Jeremiah’s experience. In the verse before, memory had brought him to deep humiliation of soul: “My soul hath them still in remembrance, and is humbled in me”; and now this same memory brought him back to life and comfort: “This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.” Like a two-edged sword, his memory first killed his pride with one edge, and then slew his despair with the other. As a general rule, if we used our memories more wisely, we might, in our very darkest distress, strike a match that would instantly light the lamp of comfort. God doesn’t need to create a new thing on the earth to bring believers back to joy; if they would prayerfully rake through the ashes of the past, they’d find light for the present; and if they would turn to the book of truth and the throne of grace, their candle would soon shine as it did before. Let’s remember the loving-kindness of the Lord, and go over his deeds of grace again. Let’s open the volume of memory, so richly illuminated with records of mercy, and we’ll soon be happy. In this way memory can be, as Coleridge calls it, “the bosom-spring of joy”; and when the divine Comforter bends it to his service, it can be first among earthly comforters.

modern:
“Be ye angry, and sin not.” There can hardly be any goodness in someone who isn’t angry at sin; whoever loves truth must hate every false way. How our Lord Jesus hated sin when the temptation came! Three times it attacked him in different forms, but every time he met it with, “Get thee behind me, Satan.” He hated it in others, no less fiercely because he showed his hatred more often in tears of pity than in words of rebuke. Yet what language could be more stern, more like Elijah, than the words, “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer.” He hated wickedness so much that he bled to wound it to the heart. He died that it might die; he was buried so that he might bury it in his tomb; and he rose so that he might trample it under his feet forever.

Christ is in the gospel, and that gospel is opposed to wickedness in every shape. Wickedness dresses up in fine clothes and imitates the language of holiness; but the commands of Jesus, like his famous whip of small cords, chase it out of the temple and won’t tolerate it in the church. So too, in the heart where Jesus reigns, what war there is between Christ and Belial! And when our Redeemer comes to be our Judge, those thundering words, “Depart, ye cursed,” which are really only a continuation of his life’s teaching about sin, will show how he loathes evil. As warm as his love for sinners is, so hot is his hatred of sin; as perfect as his righteousness is, so complete will be the destruction of every form of wickedness. O glorious champion of right and destroyer of wrong, this is why God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.

notes.note: “Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows” ([[Ps.45.7|Psalm 45:7]]).

modern:
If the man who rebuilt Jericho was cursed, how much more the man who works to bring back Roman Catholicism among us. In our fathers’ days the gigantic walls of Roman Catholicism fell by the power of their faith, the perseverance of their efforts, and the blast of their gospel trumpets; and now there are some who would rebuild that accursed system on its old foundation. O Lord, be pleased to defeat their unrighteous efforts, and pull down every stone they build. It should be a serious business with us to be thoroughly cleansed of every error that tends to foster the spirit of Roman Catholicism; and when we’ve swept our own house clean, we should try in every way to oppose its all too rapid spread abroad, in the church and in the world. This last can be done in secret by earnest prayer, and in public by firm testimony. We must warn, with wise boldness, those who lean toward the errors of Rome; we must teach the young gospel truth, and tell them of the black deeds of Roman Catholicism in times gone by. We must help spread the light more thoroughly through the land, for priests, like owls, hate daylight.

Are we doing all we can for Jesus and the gospel? If not, our neglect plays into the hands of priestcraft. What are we doing to spread the Bible, which is the Pope’s bane and poison? Are we sending out good, sound gospel writings? Luther once said, “The devil hates goose quills”; and no doubt he has good reason, for ready writers, with the Holy Spirit’s blessing, have done his kingdom a great deal of damage. If the thousands who will read this short word tonight do all they can to hinder the rebuilding of this accursed Jericho, the Lord’s glory will spread among the sons of men. Reader, what can you do? What will you do?

notes.note: After Jericho fell, Joshua laid a curse on anyone who rebuilt it ([[Josh.6.26|Joshua 6:26]]). It came true in Ahab’s day, when Hiel rebuilt the city at the cost of his sons ([[1Kgs.16.34|1 Kings 16:34]]).

modern:
A little thorn can cause a lot of pain. A little cloud can hide the sun. Little foxes spoil the vines; and little sins do damage to the tender heart. These little sins burrow into the soul and fill it so full of what Christ hates that he won’t have any comforting fellowship with us. A great sin can’t destroy a Christian, but a little sin can make him miserable. Jesus won’t walk with his people unless they drive out every known sin. He says, “If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.” Some Christians very seldom enjoy their Savior’s presence. Why is that? Surely it must be painful for a loving child to be separated from his father. Are you a child of God, and yet satisfied to go on without seeing your Father’s face? What! You, the bride of Christ, and content without his company! Surely you’ve fallen into a sad state, for the faithful bride of Christ mourns like a dove without her mate when he has left her.

Ask the question, then: what has driven Christ away from you? He hides his face behind the wall of your sins. That wall can be built of *little* pebbles as easily as of great stones. The sea is made of drops; the rocks are made of grains; and the sea that separates you from Christ may be filled with the drops of your little sins, and the rock that has nearly wrecked your boat may have been built by the daily work of the coral insects of your little sins. If you want to live with Christ, and walk with Christ, and see Christ, and have fellowship with Christ, beware of “the little foxes that spoil the vines, for our vines have tender grapes.” Jesus invites you to go *with him* and catch them. Like Samson, he will surely catch the foxes at once and easily. Go hunting with him.

modern:
Christian, what do you have to do with sin? *Hasn’t it cost you enough already*? Burned child, will you play with fire? What! When you’ve already been between the lion’s jaws, will you step into his den a second time? Haven’t you had enough of the old serpent? Didn’t he once poison all your veins? And will you play over the asp’s hole and put your hand in the viper’s den a second time? Oh, don’t be so mad, so foolish! Did sin ever give you real pleasure? Did you find solid satisfaction in it? If so, go back to your old drudgery and wear the chain again, if you enjoy it. But since sin never gave you what it promised, but deceived you with lies, don’t be caught a second time by the old bird-catcher. Be free, and let the memory of your former slavery stop you from going into the net again!

*Sin goes against the purposes of eternal love*, which all aim at your purity and holiness; so don’t work against your Lord’s purposes. Another thought should hold you back from sin: *Christians can never sin cheaply*; they pay a heavy price for wrongdoing. Sin destroys peace of mind, clouds fellowship with Jesus, hinders prayer and brings darkness over the soul; so don’t be the serf and slave of sin. There’s a higher argument still: each time you “serve sin,” you have “*Crucified the Lord afresh, and put him to an open shame*.” Can you bear that thought? Oh, if you’ve fallen into some particular sin today, perhaps my Master has sent this warning this evening to bring you back before you’ve slid very far. Turn to Jesus again; he hasn’t forgotten his love for you; his grace is still the same. Come to his footstool with weeping and repentance, and you’ll be received into his heart once more; you’ll be set on a rock again, and your steps will be made firm.

modern: David crossed that gloomy brook as he fled with his mourning company from his traitor son. The man after God’s own heart wasn’t spared trouble; in fact, his life was full of it. He was both the Lord’s Anointed and the Lord’s Afflicted. So why should we expect to escape? The noblest of our race have waited at sorrow’s gates with ashes on their heads; why then should we complain as though some strange thing had happened to us?

The *King* of kings himself wasn’t given a more cheerful or royal road. He crossed the filthy ditch of the Kidron, through which the filth of Jerusalem flowed. God had one Son without sin, but not a single child without the rod. It’s a great joy to believe that Jesus was tempted in every way, just as we are. What is our Kidron this morning? Is it a faithless friend, a sad bereavement, a slanderous accusation, a dark foreboding? The King has crossed all these. Is it bodily pain, poverty, persecution or contempt? The King has gone before us over each of these Kidrons. “In all our afflictions he was afflicted.” The idea that our trials are strange must be banished at once and forever, for he who is the Head of all saints knows by experience the grief we think so unusual. All the citizens of Zion must be free members of the Honorable Company of Mourners, of which Prince Immanuel is Head and Captain.

Though David was brought low, he still returned to his city in triumph, and David’s Lord rose victorious from the grave; so let’s be of good courage, for we too will win the day. We’ll yet draw water with joy out of the wells of salvation, though for now we have to pass by the poisonous streams of sin and sorrow. Courage, soldiers of the cross! The King himself triumphed after crossing the Kidron, and so will you.

modern:
Humbling as the statement is, the fact is certain: we’re all suffering, more or less, from the disease of sin. What a comfort to know we have a great Physician who is both able and willing to heal us! Let’s think about him for a while tonight. His cures are very *quick*: there’s life in a look at him. His cures are *radical*: he strikes at the root of the disease; and so his cures are sure and certain. He never fails, and *the disease never comes back*. There’s no relapse where Christ heals; no fear that his patients will just be patched up for a while. He makes new people of them: he gives them a new heart too, and puts a right spirit within them.

He’s skilled in *all* diseases. Doctors usually have some *specialty*. They may know a little about almost all our aches and pains, but there’s usually one disease they’ve studied more than all the others. But Jesus Christ knows the whole of human nature thoroughly. He’s as much at home with one sinner as with another, and he has never yet met an unusual case that was difficult for him. He has had extraordinary tangles of strange diseases to deal with, but he has known exactly, with one glance of his eye, how to treat the patient. He’s the only universal doctor, and the medicine he gives is the only true cure-all, healing in every single case. Whatever our spiritual illness may be, we should go at once to this divine Physician. There’s no brokenness of heart that Jesus can’t bind up. “His blood cleanseth from all sin.” We only have to think of the multitudes who have been rescued from all kinds of diseases through the power and virtue of his touch, and we’ll gladly put ourselves in his hands. We trust him, and sin dies; we love him, and grace lives; we wait for him, and grace is strengthened; we see him as he is, and grace is perfected forever.
